a4187.speech: said officially that there was agreement “on the urgent need to resolve the conflict with Ukraine peacefully”.

a4187.speaker: Vladimir Putin, President of Russia
a4187.name: Vladimir Putin
a4187.title: President of Russia
a4187.speech: said Russia's relationship with South Africa was a strategic, equal partnership and stressed that Russia attached particular importance to expanding ties with the African continent.

a4187.speaker: Vladimir Putin, President of Russia
a4187.name: Vladimir Putin
a4187.title: President of Russia
a4187.speech: After an earlier bilateral meeting with Xi, called him a dear friend and cooperation between China and Russia “one of the main stabilising factors in the world”.

a4187.speaker: Xi Jinping, President of China
a4187.name: Xi Jinping
a4187.title: President of China
a4187.speech: concurred that the friendship would endure in a world in flux, and added a call for a de-escalation in the conflict in Ukraine.

a4187.speaker: Brics summit declaration (formal document released Wednesday)
a4187.name: Brics summit declaration (formal document released Wednesday)
a4187.speech: spoke to several conflicts around the world. It called for a ceasefire and respect for international law in Gaza and expressed “alarm over the situation in southern Lebanon”. On Ukraine, the text stressed that all nations should act in line with the UN Charter and added: “We note with appreciation relevant proposals of mediation and good offices, aimed at a peaceful resolution of the conflict through dialogue and diplomacy.” It then went on to recall, in paragraph 23, the UN General Assembly's annual resolution to combat “the glorification of Nazism, neo-Nazism” and other forms of racism and xenophobia.

a4187.speaker: Delegate (anonymous)
a4187.name: Delegate (anonymous)
a4187.speech: said it was Putin's revenge, because though members could but only agree with the principle the reference was plainly inserted as a reminder of his claim that Ukraine is a “neo-Nazi regime”.

a4187.speaker: South African official (anonymous)
a4187.name: South African official (anonymous)
a4187.speech: said the common perception that Russia, China and, of late, Iran were intent on using the bloc as an axis to challenge US dominance was a misreading that chose to interpret the forum's raison d'etre in light of global shifts that happened long after it was formed, initially to optimise investment opportunities. “Besides, Brics is simply too diverse, and this characterisation fails to take into account the tension between members. Not only the deep long-standing tension between China and India but the strife within Latin America, for example around Venezuela” ; “And it completely ignores the fact that India and the UAE are very comfortable having close ties with the US and will strive to maintain those. So it can never be that. Brics is not anti-Western, and perhaps those who chose to define it as such do so because they insist on seeing the world through the prism of the West.”

a4187.speaker: Brics summit declaration (formal document)
a4187.name: Brics summit declaration (formal document)
a4187.speech: called “for a more equitable, just, democratic and balanced multipolar world order”. Members reaffirmed “our support for a comprehensive reform of the United Nations, including its security council, with a view to making it more democratic, representative, effective and efficient, and to increase the representation of developing countries in the council's memberships”, which would allow the security council not only to respond to global challenges but to “support the legitimate aspirations of emerging and developing countries from Africa, Asia and Latin America, including Brics countries, to play a greater role in international affairs, in particular in the United Nations, including its security council”.

a4187.speaker: Sanusha Naidoo, political analyst
a4187.name: Sanusha Naidoo
a4187.title: political analyst
a4187.speech: said the summit marked a moment of reflection among nations who diverge on many burning issues as to their place and possible common purpose in a shifting world order. “Brics is, in some way, not seen as an alliance, but as a forum. It is about this consensus underpinned by the right to agree to disagree. At the point where we are now, the international system is in this unpredictable spectrum and what do you do? So the question would be: how do countries utilise this space? There is also a fear of not wanting to be caught in the crosswinds of what could become a serious global debt crisis.”

a4187.speaker: South African official (anonymous)
a4187.name: South African official (anonymous)
a4187.speech: said: “The presidency of Brazil will deal with that exclusively. They will take forward the issue of a payment system that will deal with trading in local currencies.”

a4289.speaker: United Nations
a4289.name: United Nations
a4289.speech: Said Tuesday that more than 84,000 people have been affected by flash floods in Somalia since mid-April, leaving at least 17 people killed.

a4289.speaker: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a4289.name: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a4289.speech: Said Jubaland, Hirshabelle, South West, Galmudug, Puntland states and Banadir region — which includes capital Mogadishu — were most impacted, leaving more than 8,100 people displaced ; “Critical infrastructure has been damaged,” it added, noting that water points had been submerged and almost 200 latrines were destroyed ; “The rains significantly impacted internally displaced people,” OCHA said, citing local authorities.

a4289.speaker: UN report / meteorologists
a4289.name: UN report / meteorologists
a4289.speech: According to the UN report, meteorologists have warned that more rain is expected in the coming days across southern and central Somalia.

a4517.speaker: Joe Biden, outgoing US President
a4517.name: Joe Biden
a4517.title: outgoing US President
a4517.speech: Expressed his concerns about the "fragility of democracy" in America, which he attributes to the weakening of institutional "guardrails" under Republican control; in an hour-long interview recorded in the Oval Office and broadcast by MSNBC, denounced a worrying drift towards an "oligarchy" dominated by a handful of the ultra-rich, among them Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg, whom he accuses of supporting the Republican camp ; declared: "I am genuinely concerned about the level of fragility of democracy," while criticising the concentration of powers in the hands of the Republicans, affecting the executive, the legislative and the judiciary, and recalled the importance of institutional balance: "There is an independent Supreme Court, but it must be accountable. (...) You are the boss, but you cannot dictate everything." ; warned against the actions of the Trumpists, who, according to him, "seem to be cutting it into little pieces"; in an earlier speech had denounced the formation of an "oligarchy" threatening the fundamental rights and freedoms of Americans ; on MSNBC also criticised the growing grip of multibillionaires on the media and the economy.

a4517.speaker: Joe Biden, outgoing US President (on international crises)
a4517.name: Joe Biden
a4517.title: outgoing US President (on international crises)
a4517.speech: Addressed the conflicts in Ukraine and Gaza; asserted that he had played a decisive role in the truce agreement between Israel and Hamas, while rejecting the idea of any direct contact with Donald Trump on the subject; supporting his "friend" Benjamin Netanyahu, stated that he had nevertheless warned Israel not to resort to massive bombardment: "I told them: 'Bibi, you can't drop a carpet of bombs.'" ; on Ukraine, said that Russia had suffered "670,000 casualties" since the 2022 invasion, while judging that Vladimir Putin would not achieve the victory he had hoped for.

a4611.speaker: Joana Rosa, Minister of Justice of Cabo Verde
a4611.name: Joana Rosa
a4611.title: Minister of Justice of Cabo Verde
a4611.speech: Disclosed, during the inauguration of the listening room at the Criminal Investigation Department of the Judicial Police in Mindelo, that the government wants to extend the listening rooms to other islands: “We have developed this project, which is a pioneering one in Cape Verde and which will be extended to the other islands, namely where we have a higher incidence of sexual abuse and exploitation against children. In a second phase we will be working on the project, extending it to Santo Antão and Fogo. This is a project which aims to care for children when they are raped or in situations of mistreatment. A humanised project of care.”

a4611.speaker: Joana Rosa, Minister of Justice of Cabo Verde
a4611.name: Joana Rosa
a4611.title: Minister of Justice of Cabo Verde
a4611.speech: Explains that the prevention side of violence against minors is also being worked on: “That is why we are working on the legislative package, the legal regime for children and adolescents at risk, aiming to create an environment of protection, in general, for children in situations of vulnerability, whether raped, mistreated or subjected to other situations that could endanger the physical and psychological wellbeing of the child.” ; says the project was designed so that the hearings conducted in the listening rooms have legal validity, allowing the child to be heard only once, and that victims will also have protection measures so that situations of violence are not repeated.

a4611.speaker: Margaret McElligott, Minister-Counsellor of the United States of America in Cabo Verde
a4611.name: Margaret McElligott
a4611.title: Minister-Counsellor of the United States of America in Cabo Verde
a4611.speech: Highlights the importance of the project in supporting children and adolescents who are victims of abuse: “My government is very proud of this project, which laid the foundations for a justice system more geared towards children who are victims of sexual abuse, through the listening rooms. The implementation of strong awareness campaigns, training for the teams that care for these children and the development of a procedures guide already distributed to all the entities that work with victims.”

a4621.speaker: Official humanitarian response plan of the government and the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a4621.name: Official humanitarian response plan of the government and the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a4621.speech: States that roughly 1.5 million people will need humanitarian assistance in 2023, of whom 1.1 million of the most vulnerable are targeted for aid.

a4621.speaker: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a4621.name: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a4621.speech: Says that mobilising resources remains a challenge, and the UN warns that the lack of funding could have “serious consequences,” leaving vulnerable populations exposed to climate risks and disease and without protection, jeopardising repatriation efforts and livelihoods ; “Breaking the cycle of epidemics will be difficult without an emergency health response and strengthened access to water, sanitation and hygiene.”

a4621.speaker: John Agbor, interim United Nations Resident Coordinator in Burundi
a4621.name: John Agbor
a4621.title: interim United Nations Resident Coordinator in Burundi
a4621.speech: Said in a statement: “Our humanitarian response for Burundi in 2023 is the result of an in-depth analysis of the needs and challenges facing the most vulnerable populations.” He stresses that together with the government and humanitarian and development partners, “we can work towards durable solutions to improve the quality of life of these populations and build a more resilient future. We are all united by a common cause: saving lives and doing everything to leave no one behind.”

a4621.speaker: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a4621.name: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a4621.speech: Says Burundi is highly vulnerable to climate change and that natural disasters have led to significant internal displacement, and considers coordination essential to responding to the humanitarian crisis, with UN agencies continuing to support the humanitarian country team, partners and the government through needs assessments, monitoring and reporting ; “Promoting a well-funded response and a dignified return of refugees will also continue to be a priority.”

a4621.speaker: United Nations
a4621.name: United Nations
a4621.speech: According to the UN, nearly 675,000 people received humanitarian aid last year, or 70% of the initial target, an achievement resulting from joint efforts by humanitarian partners, the government of Burundi and donors.

a4654.speaker: Abdel Fattah Al-Sisi, Egyptian President
a4654.name: Abdel Fattah Al-Sisi
a4654.title: Egyptian President
a4654.speech: warning of “unimaginable instability” in the instance of any change to the country’s self-ascribed water share to the Nile waters.

a4695.speaker: Judge Bernie Griesel, Western Cape High Court
a4695.name: Judge Bernie Griesel
a4695.title: Western Cape High Court
a4695.speech: Wrote in his judgment that: “In light of the evidence revealed in this case the applicants (Independent) have in my view made out a compelling case in support of their claim for access to the document.” ; noted that not all the information contained in the Nel report (dubbed the “Rasool report”), may pertain to the brown-envelope scandal, and since the ANC had not offered to provide the relevant sections of the report, but instead sought to exclude the entire document from the public domain, ruled that the court be granted a full copy of the report.

a4695.speaker: Gasant Abarder, Cape Argus executive editor
a4695.name: Gasant Abarder
a4695.title: Cape Argus executive editor
a4695.speech: “We will be satisfied with receiving the content of the report only pertaining to the brown-envelope saga. The report apparently has other content not related or relevant to the brown-envelope case. I will be satisfied because we applied for the report on the ground that we believed it was exclusively related to the brown-envelope case.” ; said he was pleased that the court had found in Independent’s favour ; “The Cape Argus is committed to getting to the bottom of the brown-envelope saga for two reasons. Firstly, a senior public representative in his capacity as premier has been accused of paying Cape Argus journalists – both of whom have since resigned from the newspaper – to pursue his political agenda. The public has the right to know the truth. The second reason is to safeguard the integrity of the newspaper, since ANC members are claiming that other journalists still in our employ benefited financially as a result of writing stories favourable to Rasool’s political agenda.”

a4695.speaker: Gasant Abarder, Cape Argus executive editor
a4695.name: Gasant Abarder
a4695.title: Cape Argus executive editor
a4695.speech: On access to information: “John Yeld, senior journalist at the Cape Argus, made the original request on 23 August 2010 – as a request to a public body – and submitted a second PAIA application in March 2011 – as a request to a private body. Both aforementioned requests were ignored by the ANC. The Act states that if a PAIA request is ignored, it should be regarded as having been refused. This opened the door for an application in the Western Cape High Court.” ; “I think that the free flow of information is increasingly at risk. We have a constitutionally protected duty as the media to relay information from the government and act as a watchdog to inform the public so that they can hold the government accountable. I believe there are many hindrances to the free flow of information and the quality of information we receive from the government. The Cape Argus has had a number of very negative experiences with government departments and their treatment of PAIA applications. Many of them are treated with disdain and the most basic requirement, of responding to a PAIA application within 30 days, is often not even adhered to. Government departments are forcing journalists to resort to PAIA to get information that should be freely available and in the public domain. It is costly and time-consuming and I believe that the Human Rights Commission, which has an oversight role in terms of the compliance by government departments to PAIA applications, should take a harder line to enforce compliance.”

a4695.speaker: Gasant Abarder, Cape Argus executive editor
a4695.name: Gasant Abarder
a4695.title: Cape Argus executive editor
a4695.speech: On the Protection of State Information Bill: felt that, should the secrecy bill be passed in its current form, it could hamper access to information even further ; “It depends on the content of the information and to what extent agencies of state security would use the bill to classify information. In the case of the arms deal, if the bill was around, the government could have deemed the entire deal a state secret and the public would not have been able to know the truth about how their tax rands were spent and with whom our government was carrying out transactions. People have been convicted and jailed in this country for receiving bribes related to the arms deal. These kinds of prosecutions may never have seen the light of day had the arms deal been declared a state secret under the Protection of State Information Bill.”

a4695.speaker: Murray Hunter, national coordinator of the Right2Know Campaign
a4695.name: Murray Hunter
a4695.title: national coordinator of the Right2Know Campaign
a4695.speech: “PAIA is meant to ensure that citizens get access to information; (but) it’s often used by government departments simply as another obstacle to access to information. There is a missing puzzle piece, which is the political will to implement PAIA.”

a4695.speaker: South Africa’s commitment to open government under the Open Governance Partnership (document)
a4695.name: South Africa’s commitment to open government under the Open Governance Partnership (document)
a4695.speech: In the “efforts to date” section, states: “To promote transparency in South Africa, government has – among other legislation – enacted the Promotion of Access to Information Act in 2000 to ensure that information on government activities and decisions are freely available to the public. PAIA seeks to promote a culture of transparency and accountability in public and private bodies and to actively promote a society in which the people of South Africa have effective access to information to enable them to more fully exercise and protect all of their rights.”

a4743.speaker: Donald Trump, President of the United States
a4743.name: Donald Trump
a4743.title: President of the United States
a4743.speech: On Sunday harshly criticised the Russian and Ukrainian Presidents, Vladimir Putin and Volodymyr Zelensky, expressing his frustration at the stance adopted by the two leaders; while admitting that “much progress” had been made, he acknowledged that “there is tremendous hatred” between the two men, and said he was “angry” that Putin had questioned Zelensky’s credibility.

a4743.speaker: Guo Jiakun, spokesperson of the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs
a4743.name: Guo Jiakun
a4743.title: spokesperson of the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs
a4743.speech: Emphasised Beijing’s position of neutrality in the conflict: “We always believe that dialogue and negotiation are the only viable way out of the crisis. China’s cooperation with Russia is not aimed at third parties and should not be affected by third parties,” he said at a press conference.

a4743.speaker: Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs (spokesperson / announcement of the trip)
a4743.name: Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs (spokesperson / announcement of the trip)
a4743.speech: China did not mention Ukraine when it announced Wang’s trip and said only that the two countries “continue to deepen parallel strategic coordination and to expand practical cooperation in various fields,” as well as to “defend the basic norms governing international relations” ; “The Chinese side is willing to take this visit as an opportunity to work with the Russian side (...) on international and regional issues of common interest.”

a4743.speaker: Xi Jinping, Chinese President
a4743.name: Xi Jinping
a4743.title: Chinese President
a4743.speech: Has stressed on several occasions that maintaining robust relations with Russia is a “strategic choice” for Beijing.

a4823.speaker: Lisa Johnson, US ambassador to Namibia
a4823.name: Lisa Johnson
a4823.title: US ambassador to Namibia
a4823.speech: According to the ambassador, Namibia, through the ministry of trade and other stakeholders, prioritised the numerous products to support diversification of exports from Namibia to the US; these products include meat and meat products, dates, specialty foods, leather handbags, handicrafts, accessories and cosmetics ; “The US government will continue to support Namibian firms with market entry and entry-enhancing services to meet the US market entry requirements and increase exports from the priority sectors.”

a4823.speaker: Lucia Iipumbu, Namibian Minister of Trade
a4823.name: Lucia Iipumbu
a4823.title: Namibian Minister of Trade
a4823.speech: hopes Namibia will be able to maximise AGOA’s trade potential in trade, investments and skills transfer, remarks made at the launch of the utilisation strategy ; stated that Namibia’s efforts to fast-track the crafting of the strategy was ignited in 2019 during an AGOA forum in Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire: “It was also at this platform where we were informed of the possible extension of this very important framework. Now, with a strategy in place, we will unleash the full potential market the USA has to offer.”

a4823.speaker: Lucia Iipumbu, Namibian Minister of Trade
a4823.name: Lucia Iipumbu
a4823.title: Namibian Minister of Trade
a4823.speech: said the strategy concludes with a proposed action plan, covering implementation, monitoring and evaluation framework as well as an institutional structure; added the strategy hinges on a number of national policy documents, particularly the outward looking Growth at Home Strategy (Namibia’s Execution Strategy for Industrialisation), which is the implementation strategy for the country’s industrial policy.

a4869.speaker: Mary Olive Smith '88, documentary filmmaker and owner of Flying Pup Productions
a4869.name: Mary Olive Smith '88
a4869.title: documentary filmmaker and owner of Flying Pup Productions
a4869.speech: Says the path to her art was both obscured and illuminated by her varied passions: "I was given the advice that sometimes the policy line wouldn't align with my heart. I had always been involved with film and music, and I knew that was truly what filled my heart, so I kept following my passions, and everything fell into place. It turned out I had knack for the technical and logistical side of filmmaking - the grind of it all. I was never doing it for the glamour; I love the day to day."

a4869.speaker: Mary Olive Smith '88, documentary filmmaker and owner of Flying Pup Productions
a4869.name: Mary Olive Smith '88
a4869.title: documentary filmmaker and owner of Flying Pup Productions
a4869.speech: Says A Walk to Beautiful, about women in Ethiopia devastated by obstetric fistula, is both a story of healing and hope: "By far, it was the best experience of my life. There's something about childbirth that is universal - you can go to the most remote part of the world and connect with another mother."

a4869.speaker: Mary Olive Smith '88, documentary filmmaker and owner of Flying Pup Productions
a4869.name: Mary Olive Smith '88
a4869.title: documentary filmmaker and owner of Flying Pup Productions
a4869.speech: On shifting to shorter freelance pieces: "I've always tried to tell the in-depth story no matter how long the end result is. The challenge of adapting my storytelling technique into very short pieces was fascinating. I still prefer long form, but I learned you actually can tell a lot in a short time."

a4869.speaker: Mary Olive Smith '88, documentary filmmaker and owner of Flying Pup Productions
a4869.name: Mary Olive Smith '88
a4869.title: documentary filmmaker and owner of Flying Pup Productions
a4869.speech: On filming the Safe Streets organization in drug-ridden Baltimore neighbourhoods for the PBS series NOVA: "Culturally, it was the most difficult thing I've ever done. I had to gain trust from people who have lived very different lives from my own."

a4869.speaker: Mary Olive Smith '88, documentary filmmaker and owner of Flying Pup Productions
a4869.name: Mary Olive Smith '88
a4869.title: documentary filmmaker and owner of Flying Pup Productions
a4869.speech: "I can't work for free, but I wish I could. I feel lucky to get to work on these issues and tell important stories. Whether I'm in Baltimore or Ethiopia, I listen with sincerity to what people have to say. I'm 53 now, and I hope I'll keep making films for another 30 years. People in my field tend to never quit."

a4869.speaker: USAID study
a4869.name: USAID study
a4869.speech: Documented an estimated 36,000 to 39,000 women in Ethiopia live with obstetric fistula, with more than 3,000 additional new cases occurring each year.

a4890.speaker: Dillon Carroll, historian and author of Invisible Wounds
a4890.name: Dillon Carroll
a4890.title: historian and author of Invisible Wounds
a4890.speech: underscores how wars leave lasting psychological scars.

a4890.speaker: The World Bank and the IMF (published economic data)
a4890.name: The World Bank and the IMF (published economic data)
a4890.speech: publish economic data on Somalia, but these figures paint an incomplete picture; with unreliable national records and widespread tax evasion, the true state of the economy is difficult to quantify.

a5006.speaker: Ritshidze (South African community-led clinic monitoring organisation), three-month report
a5006.name: Ritshidze (South African community-led clinic monitoring organisation)
a5006.title: three-month report
a5006.speech: A report over three months shows that Pepfar cuts to HIV programmes have led to reduced staff and longer waiting times for ARV medicines; found that in areas with a high number of people with HIV, US funding cuts have led to staff shortages and overburdened clinics, and that disorganised filing systems frequently caused delays and increased waiting times.

a5006.speaker: Clinic staff surveyed by Ritshidze
a5006.name: Clinic staff surveyed by Ritshidze
a5006.speech: Nearly half the staff surveyed reported capacity in clinics had been reduced, because Pepfar-funded health workers were not working there anymore or were working less; 20% of surveyed staff said that following Pepfar cuts, there were fewer staff to provide testing and not enough test kits were available.

a5006.speaker: Clinic managers surveyed by Ritshidze
a5006.name: Clinic managers surveyed by Ritshidze
a5006.speech: 85% of managers reported that their clinics faced staffing shortages, though only one in five blamed shortages on Pepfar staff cuts.

a5006.speaker: Patients and healthcare users surveyed by Ritshidze
a5006.name: Patients and healthcare users surveyed by Ritshidze
a5006.speech: Over 60% reported that there were too few staff and that these shortages have got worse since Pepfar cuts; a fifth of healthcare users said waiting times were longer than usual (72% in Mangaung, 34% in Buffalo City), and about 35% said it had taken longer to collect ARVs since February.

a5006.speaker: Ritshidze
a5006.name: Ritshidze
a5006.speech: Said with less testing, it becomes harder to identify people with HIV who need to start or restart treatment.

a5006.speaker: South African health department
a5006.name: South African health department
a5006.speech: About 1.1 million people with HIV are not receiving treatment, according to the health department.

a5006.speaker: TAC (Treatment Action Campaign) and Ritshidze
a5006.name: TAC (Treatment Action Campaign) and Ritshidze
a5006.speech: Have recommended people be given a six-month supply of ARVs in all provinces, instead of the current one- or three-month supply.

a5006.speaker: Foster Mohale, Health department spokesperson
a5006.name: Foster Mohale
a5006.title: Health department spokesperson
a5006.speech: Had not responded by the time of publication.

a5021.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a5021.name: Donald Trump
a5021.title: US President
a5021.speech: According to Trump, such countries ‘treat us [the USA] badly’ and as a result should be punished — referring to countries that he claims impose high tariffs on American goods or have introduced other barriers to US goods.

a5021.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a5021.name: Donald Trump
a5021.title: US President
a5021.speech: Has claimed of Lesotho that ‘no one has heard of’ it.

a5240.speaker: Rawhi Fattouh, Chairman of the Palestinian National Council
a5240.name: Rawhi Fattouh
a5240.title: Chairman of the Palestinian National Council
a5240.speech: condemned the Israeli occupation army's plan to expel nearly one million Palestinians from Gaza City, which provides for forced displacement towards the coast and the southern regions, saying this crime of mass displacement reveals a plan for genocide and ethnic cleansing aimed at driving the Palestinian people from their land and destroying what remains of life in the Gaza Strip ; said in a statement published on Sunday that the occupying power's announcement that it would bring tents and shelters to the south of the Gaza Strip to accommodate those displaced from Gaza City was nothing but a cover for a larger massacre, and that the Palestinian people would be confined to less than 12 percent of the area of the Gaza Strip — a blatant violation of international law and a breach of all humanitarian conventions and values.

a5240.speaker: Rawhi Fattouh, Chairman of the Palestinian National Council
a5240.name: Rawhi Fattouh
a5240.title: Chairman of the Palestinian National Council
a5240.speech: warned against the participation of international organisations in promoting displacement and migration under the cover of humanitarian aid, in the so-called establishment of humanitarian zones on the coast or in Rafah, the "Mirage security belt" in the southern Gaza Strip, since this constitutes complicity in the displacement conspiracy ; affirmed his support for the position of UNRWA, and stressed that events in the Gaza Strip are inseparable from the ongoing crimes in the West Bank and Jerusalem, including arrests, raids and settler attacks as well as Judaisation projects and land seizures within a systematic policy of ethnic cleansing aimed at displacing the Palestinians and depriving them of their right to life and dignity.

a5240.speaker: UNRWA
a5240.name: UNRWA
a5240.speech: refuses to take part in projects aimed at the forcible displacement of the population of the Gaza Strip.

a5240.speaker: Rawhi Fattouh, Chairman of the Palestinian National Council
a5240.name: Rawhi Fattouh
a5240.title: Chairman of the Palestinian National Council
a5240.speech: said the bombing of the Baptist Hospital and the martyrdom of numerous patients and civilians constituted an outright war crime and a stain on the forehead of humanity, which stands by idly as a people is annihilated, in a disgraceful betrayal of humanity, of the right to life and of its moral, legal and international duties and responsibilities to prevent the slaughter, the bloodshed and the massacres.

a5240.speaker: Rawhi Fattouh, Chairman of the Palestinian National Council
a5240.name: Rawhi Fattouh
a5240.title: Chairman of the Palestinian National Council
a5240.speech: called on the US government to stop supporting the occupation in this aggression against the Palestinian people and to use its influence to end the greatest operation of injustice, starvation, genocide and ethnic cleansing of the past 681 days.

a5667.speaker: UN food agencies (FAO and the World Food Programme)
a5667.name: UN food agencies (FAO and the World Food Programme)
a5667.speech: Warned on Thursday of worsening hunger levels over the next seven months in many regions of the world, with Gaza, Sudan, South Sudan, Mali and Haiti of greatest concern.

a5667.speaker: Joint FAO–WFP semi-annual report (November 2024 to May 2025)
a5667.name: Joint FAO–WFP semi-annual report (November 2024 to May 2025)
a5667.speech: States that conflict and armed violence are behind most of the acute food insecurity in all the regions analysed; that extreme weather is an important factor in other regions, while economic inequality and high debt levels in many developing countries undermine governments’ capacity to respond; that humanitarian action is urgently needed to avert famine and death in the Gaza Strip, Sudan, South Sudan, Haiti and Mali; and warns that “in the absence of immediate humanitarian efforts and concerted international action to address severe access constraints and to de-escalate conflict and insecurity, famine and loss of life risk worsening” in those regions; it also lists Nigeria, Chad, Yemen, Mozambique, Burma, Syria and Lebanon as of very high concern.

a5667.speaker: The report’s authors
a5667.name: The report’s authors
a5667.speech: Recall that the report focuses on “the most serious situations” and therefore does not represent “all countries/territories experiencing high levels of acute food insecurity”.

a5667.speaker: Joint FAO–WFP semi-annual report (November 2024 to May 2025)
a5667.name: Joint FAO–WFP semi-annual report (November 2024 to May 2025)
a5667.speech: Reports that in the Gaza Strip the recent resurgence of hostilities raises fears the “catastrophe” famine scenario will materialise, with about 41% of the population, or 876,000 people, facing “emergency” level 4 hunger from November to the end of April and nearly 16%, or 345,000 people, reaching “catastrophe” levels; that in Sudan hundreds of thousands of people displaced by the conflict will continue to face famine; that in South Sudan the number of people facing famine and death is expected to have almost doubled over the four months from April to July 2024 compared with the same period in 2023, and that more than a million people were affected by severe flooding there this month; that armed violence in Haiti combined with a persistent economic crisis and hurricanes risks worsening already critical hunger levels; and that the escalating conflict in Mali, where the UN withdrew its peacekeeping mission in 2023, risks aggravating already critical levels as armed groups set up roadblocks and prevent humanitarian aid deliveries; it adds that the direct and indirect effects of conflict on food insecurity go well beyond the destruction of livestock and crops, forcing people to flee their homes, “disrupting livelihoods and incomes, limiting access to markets and causing price fluctuations as well as irregular food production and consumption”, and that extreme weather caused by the possible return of La Niña this winter could exacerbate food crises.

a5684.speaker: Jirair Ratevosian, former head of staff at Pepfar and fellow at Duke University's Global Health Institute
a5684.name: Jirair Ratevosian
a5684.title: former head of staff at Pepfar and fellow at Duke University's Global Health Institute
a5684.speech: “It's a small win within the bigger context, but nonetheless, a huge win for advocacy, and a reminder that activism is powerful and alive, and making an impact,” told Bhekisisa at last week's Conference on HIV Science in Kigali.

a5684.speaker: Mitchell Warren, head of international advocacy organisation Avac
a5684.name: Mitchell Warren
a5684.title: head of international advocacy organisation Avac
a5684.speech: “It opens the floodgates for the Trump administration to say ‘we don't want this or that in the budget that Congress approved’ ; It's trying to take the congressional power of the purse and put it in the executive branch to usurp the role of Congress in deciding how much money — and on what to spend it.”

a5684.speaker: Analysts at the Centre on Budget and Policy Priorities, Washington DC
a5684.name: Analysts at the Centre on Budget and Policy Priorities
a5684.title: Washington DC
a5684.speech: Point out that Trump wants more control over how his administration's money is spent ; explain in an analysis that over the past few months the Trump administration's main strategy has “simply been to illegally impound funds — by announcing a ‘funding freeze’ or ‘programmatic review’ with no public notice at all — and force those harmed by the impoundments to pursue relief in court”.

a5684.speaker: Mitchell Warren, head of Avac
a5684.name: Mitchell Warren
a5684.title: head of Avac
a5684.speech: Says the $400 million was part of the financial budget for 2025, but because the law gives Pepfar permission to spend money over five years, that money doesn't have to be legally spent until 2029.

a5684.speaker: Trump administration
a5684.name: Trump administration
a5684.speech: Says it's not prepared to buy HIV prevention medicine for any group other than pregnant and breastfeeding women.

a5684.speaker: Mitchell Warren, head of Avac
a5684.name: Mitchell Warren
a5684.title: head of Avac
a5684.speech: “It used to be all about evidence. Now it's all about ideology.”

a5684.speaker: Jirair Ratevosian, former head of staff at Pepfar
a5684.name: Jirair Ratevosian
a5684.title: former head of staff at Pepfar
a5684.speech: Says this moment should be used to gain Republican support to change the waiver rules, so that Pepfar money can cover more of the populations and services needed for HIV prevention, and that lenacapavir, a pricey twice-a-year anti-HIV jab, could be used to convince Republican Congress members: “Pepfar has long wanted to get countries to transition to taking more ownership [read: pay more] for their HIV responses. So now activists are arguing: ‘Preventing more new infections with the jab, will make it easier for countries to take ownership because the pandemic will be easier to manage.’”

a5684.speaker: Pepfar
a5684.name: Pepfar
a5684.speech: In December, Pepfar said it would join another organisation, the Global Fund for HIV, TB and Malaria, to buy enough lenacapavir for two million people over three years.

a5684.speaker: Mitchell Warren, head of Avac
a5684.name: Mitchell Warren
a5684.title: head of Avac
a5684.speech: “If I were in charge, I would take the $400 million and double the two million people the Global Fund is planning to cover, because that's how you build a market, prevent new infections more quickly and drive the price down.”

a5684.speaker: Mitchell Warren, head of Avac
a5684.name: Mitchell Warren
a5684.title: head of Avac
a5684.speech: “We're not going to get pre-January projects back; we have to build something different” ; “This has been the most seismic shift in democracy. We didn't think we lived in an earthquake zone, but January 20 [when Trump retook office] taught us: you need to be prepared for that earthquake and you therefore need a different infrastructure. In an earthquake you don't build back the same thing. You build better, something that is more resilient.”

a5684.speaker: Scientists (modelling studies)
a5684.name: Scientists (modelling studies)
a5684.speech: Tens of modelling studies have projected what could happen if the lost funds are not replaced.

a6109.speaker: Government of Tanzania
a6109.name: Government of Tanzania
a6109.speech: Said it will continue to fund students studying science subjects and to recognise researchers who conduct research that helps it put in place strategic plans for tackling various diseases in the country.

a6109.speaker: Dr Doto Biteko, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Energy of Tanzania
a6109.name: Dr Doto Biteko
a6109.title: Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Energy of Tanzania
a6109.speech: Said, while opening the international scientific conference organised by the Catholic University of Health and Allied Sciences (Cuhas) under the theme of One Health and Global Security in Mwanza, that the funding will enable students to study and enable the country to obtain many specialists in the health sector: "The government will continue to empower, fund and recognise researchers who perform well and publish in journals within and outside the country; keep on doing research in order to fight any type of disease."

a6109.speaker: Dr Doto Biteko, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Energy of Tanzania
a6109.name: Dr Doto Biteko
a6109.title: Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Energy of Tanzania
a6109.speech: Said more than 150 research publications published by Cuhas have helped the government put in place various strategies, including the national strategy against antimicrobial resistance; added that to ensure the country and Tanzanians are safe from diseases including epidemics, the government in collaboration with scientists has prepared the National One Health Strategic Plan 2022/27, which draws on expertise across the human health, livestock, wildlife and environment sectors in order to reduce outbreaks of zoonotic diseases, drug resistance and other health threats.

a6109.speaker: Dr Doto Biteko, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Energy of Tanzania
a6109.name: Dr Doto Biteko
a6109.title: Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Energy of Tanzania
a6109.speech: Congratulated the best national health scientist for 2024, Cuhas researcher and professor of pathogens Stephene Mshana, who has conducted more than 270 studies and is cited internationally.

a6109.speaker: Omari Kipanga, Deputy Minister of Education, Science and Technology
a6109.name: Omari Kipanga
a6109.title: Deputy Minister of Education, Science and Technology
a6109.speech: Said that through the Higher Education for Economic Transformation (HEET) project, worth more than Sh972 billion, 1,000 specialists will be trained in the health sector; said another plan to raise science and health matters in the country is the government's strategy to build a school in every region that will teach science subjects to girls in order to produce enough scientists to serve the country and the world: "The issue of developing scientists is there, we have our very big project of educational transformation for the economic field worth more than Sh972 billion; that project, among other things, will ensure that it trains more than 1,000 specialists in the health sector as well as other sectors, but great emphasis has been placed on the health sector."

a6109.speaker: Professor Erasmus Kamugisha, Vice Chancellor of Cuhas
a6109.name: Professor Erasmus Kamugisha
a6109.title: Vice Chancellor of Cuhas
a6109.speech: Presenting the conference report, asked the government, through the Higher Education Students' Loans Board (HESLB), to give loans to students studying science so that they can afford the costs of those studies, which he said are high: "In the first phase our students received a certain amount that will ease the burden of fees, so we also expect that in the next phase they will continue to receive loans to help them pay their fees and food." ; "Students studying science at health colleges pay higher fees than at other colleges, so if they do not get loans it becomes difficult to afford the fees charged at science colleges; the loans help them cushion the difficulty of paying those fees at our institutions."

a6109.speaker: Professor Mariam Mirambo, Chairperson of the conference organising committee
a6109.name: Professor Mariam Mirambo
a6109.title: Chairperson of the conference organising committee
a6109.speech: Said the conference will help students as well as local scientists get the opportunity to discuss various research matters and to gain experience of what participants from foreign countries are doing.

a6343.speaker: Eli Cohen, Israeli Energy Minister
a6343.name: Eli Cohen
a6343.title: Israeli Energy Minister
a6343.speech: Said in a short video: “I have just signed the order to immediately stop supplying electricity to the Gaza Strip.”

a6343.speaker: Hamas / Izzat al-Rishq, member of the movement's political bureau (statement)
a6343.name: Hamas / Izzat al-Rishq
a6343.title: member of the movement's political bureau (statement)
a6343.speech: Reacted by describing the act as “unacceptable” blackmail, “firmly” condemning “(Israel's) decision to cut off electricity to Gaza, after having deprived it of food, medicine and water.”

a6363.speaker: New America (think tank data) and US Africa Command (AFRICOM) statements
a6363.name: New America (think tank data) and US Africa Command (AFRICOM) statements
a6363.speech: Since the start of 2025, the U.S. has carried out at least 51 airstrikes across Somalia, more than doubling last year’s count and positioning this year to break the Trump-era record of 63 strikes set in 2019, according to data compiled by the think tank New America and verified through U.S. Africa Command (AFRICOM) statements.

a6363.speaker: Somali federal government
a6363.name: Somali federal government
a6363.speech: has welcomed Washington’s military support in its long-running fight against al-Shabaab and Islamic State-Somalia (IS-Somalia).

a6363.speaker: Rights groups, analysts, and local communities
a6363.name: Rights groups
a6363.title: analysts, and local communities
a6363.speech: say the airstrikes are increasingly undermining civilian safety, fueling resentment, and failing to prevent militant territorial gains.

a6363.speaker: Donald Trump, US President (February 1 post)
a6363.name: Donald Trump
a6363.title: US President (February 1 post)
a6363.speech: Just ten days after taking office in January 2025, Trump authorized his first Somalia airstrike, claiming it targeted ISIS leaders hiding “in caves,” a reference he made in a February 1 post.

a6363.speaker: US Africa Command (AFRICOM)
a6363.name: US Africa Command (AFRICOM)
a6363.speech: According to AFRICOM, at least 30 of the 51 airstrikes this year targeted IS-Somalia positions in Puntland’s Cal Miskaad mountains, part of Operation Hilaac, a multi-phase counterterrorism offensive led by Puntland’s security forces. The remaining strikes focused on al-Shabaab positions in central and southern regions, including Hiiraan and Jubaland.

a6363.speaker: US Africa Command (AFRICOM)
a6363.name: US Africa Command (AFRICOM)
a6363.speech: While the command pledged to continue releasing quarterly civilian harm reports, watchdog groups and Somali civil society leaders say the lack of transparency erodes accountability.

a6363.speaker: Watchdog groups and Somali civil society leaders
a6363.name: Watchdog groups and Somali civil society leaders
a6363.speech: say the lack of transparency erodes accountability, after AFRICOM suspended the publication of casualty figures in recent strike announcements.

a6363.speaker: Amnesty International
a6363.name: Amnesty International
a6363.speech: In 2019, Amnesty International accused the U.S. of possible war crimes in Somalia due to civilian deaths from drone strikes under Trump’s first term.

a6363.speaker: Victims Advocacy International
a6363.name: Victims Advocacy International
a6363.speech: Despite AFRICOM’s eventual acknowledgment of some civilian harm, no victims have been compensated, according to Victims Advocacy International, an organization seeking accountability for victims of human rights abuses in conflict zones across the globe.

a6363.speaker: Eva Buzo, executive director of Victims Advocacy International
a6363.name: Eva Buzo
a6363.title: executive director of Victims Advocacy International
a6363.speech: “The consistent lack of accountability for civilian victims of U.S. air strikes, particularly under the previous [Trump] administration, speaks volumes. It reveals a profound lack of transparency that is deeply concerning,” said Eva Buzo, the group’s executive director. “The U.S. acknowledges harm to civilians and has allocated funds, yet continues to avoid making these crucial payments,” she added.

a6363.speaker: New America and the conflict monitor Airwars (estimate)
a6363.name: New America and the conflict monitor Airwars (estimate)
a6363.speech: estimate that between 33 and 167 Somali civilians have been killed in U.S. strikes since 2007, although the exact toll remains disputed due to limited on-the-ground verification and the rural, clan-fragmented nature of affected areas.

a6363.speaker: Experts (unnamed)
a6363.name: Experts (unnamed)
a6363.speech: Experts warn that the use of patchy human intelligence in areas shaped by shifting clan dynamics, combined with the U.S.’s remote targeting model, heightens the risk of misidentification and civilian casualties.

a6363.speaker: Jethro Norman, Danish Institute for International Studies
a6363.name: Jethro Norman
a6363.title: Danish Institute for International Studies
a6363.speech: “These incidents don’t just cause resentment; they offer propaganda gold,” said Jethro Norman of the Danish Institute for International Studies. When civilians are killed or even just displaced, al-Shabaab exploits the aftermath. They move quickly to frame themselves as defenders of Somali lives and sovereignty against a foreign aggressor and a weak federal government.”

a6363.speaker: US officials (unnamed)
a6363.name: US officials (unnamed)
a6363.speech: U.S. officials said the boat [destroyed in a rare maritime strike in April] was likely part of a smuggling network linked to Yemen’s Houthi rebels.

a6363.speaker: Analysts (unnamed)
a6363.name: Analysts (unnamed)
a6363.speech: Analysts interpret the change [in engagement protocols] as part of a broader reliance on long-range airstrikes due to resource constraints and operational risk aversion.

a6363.speaker: David Sterman, New America
a6363.name: David Sterman
a6363.title: New America
a6363.speech: As New America’s David Sterman noted, the policy shift has allowed AFRICOM to conduct preemptive strikes with reduced oversight, increasing strike volume but decreasing accountability.

a6363.speaker: Jethro Norman, Danish Institute for International Studies
a6363.name: Jethro Norman
a6363.title: Danish Institute for International Studies
a6363.speech: “There’s no corresponding investment in peacebuilding or governance support,” said Norman. “Airpower can suppress, but it doesn’t transform.” ; “The gap between U.S. rhetoric and Somali reality is where al-Shabaab thrives,” said Norman. “If the Trump administration continues its drone diplomacy without local legitimacy, it will only deepen the crisis.”

a6363.speaker: Bihi Imaan Egeh, Somali Finance Minister
a6363.name: Bihi Imaan Egeh
a6363.title: Somali Finance Minister
a6363.speech: disclosed in March that the U.S. had cut funding to Danab, Somalia’s elite special forces unit trained by the U.S. military.

a6363.speaker: Analysts (unnamed)
a6363.name: Analysts (unnamed)
a6363.speech: Though Trump’s drone campaign has delivered tactical blows, analysts agree that Somalia’s long-term stability depends on more than firepower.

a6504.speaker: Rural Self-Help Development Association (local organisation supporting farmers in Lesotho)
a6504.name: Rural Self-Help Development Association (local organisation supporting farmers in Lesotho)
a6504.speech: Is warning of the risks to the country’s food security and economic prospects following the abrupt interruption of the STEPS project, which deprived thousands of poultry farms across seven districts of resources.

a6727.speaker: International Monetary Fund
a6727.name: International Monetary Fund
a6727.speech: Is anticipating an increase in funding support requests from Africa as US President Donald Trump's tariffs and aid cuts reduce options.

a6727.speaker: Abebe Aemro Selassie, director of the IMF's African Department
a6727.name: Abebe Aemro Selassie
a6727.title: director of the IMF's African Department
a6727.speech: “We live in a shock-prone world” ; “The poorest and least resilient countries are increasingly turning to institutions like ours. I don't rule out” more African countries seeking support, he told reporters Tuesday in Senegal's capital, Dakar.

a6758.speaker: Mozambican Football Federation (FMF)
a6758.name: Mozambican Football Federation (FMF)
a6758.speech: Writes on its social media page that the Mambas will face South Africa in a friendly match, within the official FIFA window, on Tuesday, 10 June 2025, at the Loftus Versfeld Stadium in Pretoria: "The match forms part of the national team's preparation plan for the upcoming official fixtures and constitutes an opportunity to strengthen the group's cohesion, as well as to assess the performance of athletes in an international competitive context." According to the FMF's note, the announcement of the 22-player squad is imminent and should include players who play abroad, since their leagues have already ended.

a6758.speaker: South Africa Football Association (SAFA)
a6758.name: South Africa Football Association (SAFA)
a6758.speech: Also confirmed, through its website, that the match between Bafana Bafana and the Mambas will take place in a friendly at the Loftus Stadium in Pretoria on Tuesday, 10 June 2025; wrote that "a few days ago, the coach of South Africa's senior men's national team, Hugo Broos, announced a preliminary squad of 41 players for the friendlies against Tanzania, to be played at the Peter Mokaba Stadium in Polokwane, Limpopo, on Friday, 6 June 2025, and Mozambique" ; "The Mamelodi Sundowns players were not selected, as they will take part in the FIFA Club World Cup, which will be played in the United States from 14 June to 13 July 2025."

a6758.speaker: Hugo Broos, coach of South Africa's senior men's national team
a6758.name: Hugo Broos
a6758.title: coach of South Africa's senior men's national team
a6758.speech: Announced a preliminary squad of 41 players for the friendlies against Tanzania and Mozambique, of whom only 23 will make the final squad, to be announced this week.

a6785.speaker: Million Masumbika, Tutume District Council chairperson
a6785.name: Million Masumbika
a6785.title: Tutume District Council chairperson
a6785.speech: Disclosed, when addressing a Full Council meeting recently, that a total of 166 human-wildlife conflict cases were received since the beginning of October to date: "Two hundred and eighty-five cases were compensated with an amount P426 000. Thirteen cases are owed an amount of P31 000." Said wild animals, particularly elephants, have destroyed farms, community dams and animal barrier fences along the road in several villages making up the district, and that lions and other predators kill and prey on livestock in many parts of the district, with Maitengwe, Dukwi and Tutume among the most affected; despite the severity of the conflicts, no human injuries were reported in the last quarter.

a6785.speaker: Million Masumbika, Tutume District Council chairperson
a6785.name: Million Masumbika
a6785.title: Tutume District Council chairperson
a6785.speech: Anticipates further incursions by elephants and other wildlife into the district as drought conditions persist: "This is a drought year, and the conditions will ultimately force elephants and other wildlife to seek water and food in areas they would not typically venture into, such as villages and human settlements. The challenges posed by wild animals particularly elephants to farmers have really had significant economic repercussions for local communities reliant on agriculture and livestock in recent years. Farmers in the district have been making severe losses."

a6785.speaker: A UK legislator and some British MPs
a6785.name: A UK legislator and some British MPs
a6785.speech: A UK legislator has come up with a member's Bill that purports to ban importation of hunting trophies into the UK, and some British MPs are pushing for a law prohibiting the importation of hunting trophies to the UK as a measure to protect endangered species.

a6880.speaker: Akinwumi Adesina, African Development Bank (AfDB) group president
a6880.name: Akinwumi Adesina
a6880.title: African Development Bank (AfDB) group president
a6880.speech: Says Africa must wean itself from aid dependency due to the dwindling global funding trend, adding that the era of free money is long gone ; in a statement following a lecture at National Open University of Nigeria, called on African economies, including Malawi, to urgently chart their future through self-reliance, strategic partnerships and leveraging its vast natural resources ; “The recent dismantling of the official development aid agency in the United States and similar anti-aid measures in other parts of Europe, means that the old development models that Africa has always relied on will no longer work.”

a6880.speaker: Akinwumi Adesina, African Development Bank (AfDB) group president
a6880.name: Akinwumi Adesina
a6880.title: African Development Bank (AfDB) group president
a6880.speech: Said Africa faces several challenges, including declining development aid, restrictive immigration policies, undervalued natural capital and the recent global tariff wars.

a6880.speaker: Simplex Chithyola Banda, Minister of Finance and Economic Affairs (Malawi)
a6880.name: Simplex Chithyola Banda
a6880.title: Minister of Finance and Economic Affairs (Malawi)
a6880.speech: Earlier said following the USaid decision, government will ensure that all services regarding HIV and Aids continue to be offered in the country’s health system.

a6880.speaker: Kondwani Hara, Centre for Social Concern project officer
a6880.name: Kondwani Hara
a6880.title: Centre for Social Concern project officer
a6880.speech: Observed that the US decision has exposed vulnerabilities of Malawi’s economy.

a6926.speaker: Nur Osman Raage, Shalanbod Administrator
a6926.name: Nur Osman Raage
a6926.title: Shalanbod Administrator
a6926.speech: "The most important thing we have learned is the decentralisation of the local administration. We also understood how important is the work of the Local Administration and that of the District Administration, and we also found out that we are all under the District Commissioner (DC). We give the DC daily reports for ease of the work."

a6926.speaker: Ibrahim Adan Ali (Najah), Governor of Lower Shabelle
a6926.name: Ibrahim Adan Ali (Najah)
a6926.title: Governor of Lower Shabelle
a6926.speech: Said the role of women in the local administration has been impressively applaudable: "Women are core part of our society. They are also an important workforce in the government. For these reasons, promoting the participation of women in the training as decision-makers was a significant aim of the training."

a6926.speaker: Aniso Heyle, female administrator, Marka District Administration
a6926.name: Aniso Heyle
a6926.title: female administrator, Marka District Administration
a6926.speech: Noted how the training empowered her to develop skills of cooperation and good governance: "This training was very informative and successful because first of all it was designed for us. As an administrator now, I am able to deliver better services for my community and for my city of Marka which was once the most preferred holiday destination in the southern Somalia."

a7042.speaker: Press office of the U.S. Consulate in Lagos (statement)
a7042.name: Press office of the U.S. Consulate in Lagos (statement)
a7042.speech: Said in a statement on Friday that, as Consul General in Lagos, Mr Swart is the senior U.S. Government representative to the Nigerian people throughout the 17 states in southern Nigeria, and that he is responsible for leading and overseeing U.S. government activities that deepen trade and investment ties, expand people-to-people connections, and advance the full range of priorities in the U.S.-Nigeria bilateral relationship across the region.

a7042.speaker: Rick Swart, U.S. Consul General in Lagos
a7042.name: Rick Swart
a7042.title: U.S. Consul General in Lagos
a7042.speech: “I am honoured to serve in Nigeria. I am excited about the opportunity to travel across the region, meet the people, experience the culture, while advancing the shared goals of making our two countries safer, stronger, and more prosperous.” ; “I thank JoEllen for her remarkable leadership and for the outstanding work she has done to promote our close partnership with the Nigerian people in the region. I look forward to working closely with Ambassador Mills and the team at the U.S. Embassy in Abuja, to further advance the shared objectives between Nigeria and the United States.”

a7150.speaker: Aisha Mafa, displaced mother of five in Gubio camp
a7150.name: Aisha Mafa
a7150.title: displaced mother of five in Gubio camp
a7150.speech: “My friends advised me to take him to the clinic at the camp, where services were free,” ; “Without the health workers, I don’t know what would have happened to my son,” ; “I take comfort to know that my children and I can get free health services here.”

a7150.speaker: Martha Sini, Local Government Area Facilitator for the mobile health team in Gubio camp
a7150.name: Martha Sini
a7150.title: Local Government Area Facilitator for the mobile health team in Gubio camp
a7150.speech: “Since we started, we’ve treated around 9000 people,” ; “Routine immunization, maternal care and clinical services are vital for protecting the health of the community, especially women and children.”

a7150.speaker: Huawa Ali, seven-months-pregnant woman displaced by the floods from Gwange district, Maiduguri
a7150.name: Huawa Ali
a7150.title: seven-months-pregnant woman displaced by the floods from Gwange district, Maiduguri
a7150.speech: “I am so grateful for this care. Without it, I wouldn’t have known if my baby was safe. Now, I feel more confident about my pregnancy,” she says.

a7150.speaker: Report distributed by the APO Group on behalf of World Health Organization (WHO) – Nigeria
a7150.name: Report distributed by the APO Group on behalf of World Health Organization (WHO) – Nigeria
a7150.speech: Stated that beyond immediate medical care, WHO also supports Borno state in enhancing surveillance activities. Over 150 community health volunteers have been deployed to conduct active case finding for priority diseases and house-to-house sensitization to improve health-seeking behaviour within the camps and host communities.

a7150.speaker: Dr Walter Mulombo, WHO Representative for Nigeria
a7150.name: Dr Walter Mulombo
a7150.title: WHO Representative for Nigeria
a7150.speech: “For the families in temporary camps, the presence of our mobile health teams offers more than just medical care, it provides hope for a healthier future, for their children’s well-being, and hope that they will overcome the challenges of displacement,” says Dr Walter Mulombo.

a7240.speaker: UNFPA (supplies data)
a7240.name: UNFPA (supplies data)
a7240.speech: Cited as the source for the figure that in 2024 these services and commodities helped avert some 9.49 million unintended pregnancies, 3.38 million abortions and 19,150 maternal deaths in the region.

a7240.speaker: 2gether 4 SRHR (joint United Nations Regional Programme) analysis
a7240.name: 2gether 4 SRHR (joint United Nations Regional Programme) analysis
a7240.speech: Analysis indicates that funding cuts will have a significant impact on health equity; increase the barriers for vulnerable populations to access services; reverse the progress made in the HIV response; impact on early and unintended pregnancies; weaken health systems; and challenge the collection of data that enables stakeholders to monitor impact, improve programming, identify gaps, and hold Governments accountable.

a7240.speaker: UNAIDS (projections)
a7240.name: UNAIDS (projections)
a7240.speech: According to UNAIDS projections, if funding is not available to fill in the gap left by PEPFAR funding cuts we can expect to see, globally, a 400 per cent increase in AIDS-related deaths, 8.7 million new HIV adult infections, an additional 3.4 million orphans made vulnerable by HIV and 350,000 new HIV infections in children by 2029. Our region will bear witness to 75 per cent of these deaths and new infections.

a7393.speaker: Communication and Public Education Unit, Parliament of Tanzania (statement)
a7393.name: Communication and Public Education Unit
a7393.title: Parliament of Tanzania (statement)
a7393.speech: Said in a statement issued on January 3, 2025 that the committee sittings, running January 6-24, 2025 in Dodoma, precede the 18th session of Parliament expected to begin on Tuesday, January 28, 2025; said that during that period the Standing Committee on Subsidiary Legislation and the Standing Committee on Public Investments (PIC) will begin sittings on January 6, 2025 while the remaining committees begin on January 13, 2025 ; “The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Public Investments (PIC) will receive and examine reports on public capital investments in order to establish whether those investments are efficient and whether they have complied with proper business procedures and guidelines.” ; “It will carry out the scrutiny of Subsidiary Legislation submitted to Parliament in the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Sessions of Parliament.” ; “Eleven sectoral Committees will receive and discuss various reports on the performance of the Government and its Institutions. In addition, the Budget Committee will receive and discuss a report on the implementation of the Government Budget for the half-year period (July - December 2024).”

a7474.speaker: Global Soft Power Index 2025, Brand Finance
a7474.name: Global Soft Power Index 2025
a7474.title: Brand Finance
a7474.speech: One of the most notable findings from the survey is that the US has retained its position as the top-ranked soft power state, as it was in the 2024 edition; the 2025 edition evaluated all 193 United Nations member states, drawing on data from a global sample of over 170,000 respondents across more than 100 markets; China has now risen to second place, overtaking the United Kingdom, with Japan, Germany, France, Canada, Switzerland, Italy and the UAE maintaining their 2024 rankings from fourth to tenth; Egypt, South Africa, Morocco, Nigeria and Algeria are the highest-ranked African states in the index.

a7474.speaker: Portland's Soft Power 30 Index (2019)
a7474.name: Portland's Soft Power 30 Index (2019)
a7474.speech: In 2019, France overtook the US as the leading soft power state.
